claim: Mean precise editing efficiencies >90% were obtained on primary cord blood HSPCs with minimal toxicity and without observed off-target editing.
source: Through an optimization of guide RNA delivery, donor design, and additives, we have now obtained mean precise editing efficiencies >90% on primary cord blood HSCPs with minimal toxicity and without observed off-target editing.
evidence: The abstract directly states the achieved editing efficiency with supporting data shown in figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: The addition of the DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648 was a main protocol modification needed to achieve high editing efficiencies.
source: The main protocol modifications needed to achieve such high efficiencies were the addition of the DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648, and the inclusion of spacer-breaking silent mutations in the donor in addition to mutations disrupting the PAM sequence.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies AZD7648 as a main protocol modification, with supporting experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The inclusion of spacer-breaking silent mutations in the donor in addition to mutations disrupting the PAM sequence was a main protocol modification needed to achieve high editing efficiencies.
source: The main protocol modifications needed to achieve such high efficiencies were the addition of the DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648, and the inclusion of spacer-breaking silent mutations in the donor in addition to mutations disrupting the PAM sequence.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies spacer-breaking silent mutations as a main protocol modification, with supporting experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy.
source: Critically, editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy, did not substantially distort the hierarchy or affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays or the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing no significant differences in editing efficiencies across phenotypically defined progenitor compartments.

claim: Editing did not substantially distort the progenitor hierarchy.
source: Critically, editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy, did not substantially distort the hierarchy or affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays or the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing minimal changes in progenitor phenotypes.

claim: Editing did not affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays.
source: Critically, editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy, did not substantially distort the hierarchy or affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays or the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E showing no changes in colony type distribution.

claim: Editing did not affect the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells.
source: Critically, editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy, did not substantially distort the hierarchy or affect lineage outputs in colony-forming cell assays or the frequency of high self-renewal potential long-term culture initiating cells.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3I showing no significant difference in highly proliferative clone frequencies.

claim: Overall editing and zygosity can be tuned by adding in defined mixtures of mutant and wild-type donors.
source: As modelling of many diseases requires heterozygosity, we also demonstrated that the overall editing and zygosity can be tuned by adding in defined mixtures of mutant and wild-type donors.
evidence: The abstract states this claim, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing controlled zygosity based on donor ratios.

claim: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the default pathway for DNA repair after CRISPR/Cas-induced breaks.
source: While this strategy can function, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) which results in random insertions and deletions (indels) is the default pathway, as HDR can only operate in the S and G2 phase of the cell cycle (Lin et al., 2014; Heyer et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Lin et al., 2014; Heyer et al., 2010) to support this established biological fact.

claim: HDR can only operate in the S and G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: While this strategy can function, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) which results in random insertions and deletions (indels) is the default pathway, as HDR can only operate in the S and G2 phase of the cell cycle (Lin et al., 2014; Heyer et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Lin et al., 2014; Heyer et al., 2010) to support this established biological fact.

claim: Most HDR-mediated editing strategies in primary human stem and progenitor populations achieve efficiencies in the range of 10–20%.
source: As such, the efficiency of HDR-mediated editing, particularly in relevant primary human stem and progenitor populations remains limited, with most strategies achieving efficiencies in the range of 10–20% (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018) to support this claim about typical editing efficiencies.

claim: Multiple clinical trials using CRISPR/Cas-based editing strategies are currently ongoing.
source: Despite such limited efficiencies, multiple clinical trials using CRISPR/Cas-based editing strategies are currently ongoing, reinforcing the extreme interest in the area (Porteus et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Porteus et al., 2022) to support this claim about ongoing clinical trials.

claim: Intracellular donor concentration has been shown to correlate to HDR efficiency.
source: One simple method to improve HDR efficiency involves increasing the concentration of donor template as intracellular donor concentration has been shown to correlate to HDR efficiency (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Lee et al., 2017) to support this claim about donor concentration effects.

claim: High concentrations of donor AAV have been shown to improve the efficiency of HDR in HSPCs.
source: Indeed, in HSPCs high concentrations of donor AAV have been shown to improve the efficiency of HDR, though likely at the cost of cell viability as, while not measured directly, a subsequent live-dead selection was performed in the study (Tran et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Tran et al., 2022) to support this claim about AAV concentration effects.

claim: Transient knockdown of p53 by siRNA was shown to improve survival of human hematopoietic stem cells.
source: To this end, transient knockdown of p53 by siRNA was shown to improve survival of human hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), though not directly modulate the HDR editing efficiency (Lehnertz et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Lehnertz et al., 2021) to support this claim about p53 knockdown effects.

claim: Inhibition of 53BP1 has been shown to improve the editing efficiency in HSPCs reaching up to ~60%.
source: Interestingly, Inhibition of 53BP1 which has the additional effect of NHEJ inhibition has been shown to improve the editing efficiency in these cells reaching up to ~60% (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about 53BP1 inhibition effects.

claim: Edited cells retained their functional stem cell capacity following the editing protocol with 53BP1 inhibition.
source: Critically, both studies demonstrate that edited cells retained their functional stem cell capacity (long-term engraftment in xenotransplantation) following the editing protocol, with efficiencies similar to pre-transplant measurements.
evidence: The introduction references studies (De Ravin et al., 2021; Lehnertz et al., 2021) demonstrating functional stem cell capacity retention.

claim: M3814 inhibitor of DNA-PK has been shown to increase editing efficiencies up to 80–90% in primary human T cells.
source: Another small molecule inhibitor of NHEJ, M3814 that inhibits DNA-PK, has been shown to increase editing efficiencies up to 80–90% in primary human T cells (Shy et al., 2023).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (Shy et al., 2023) to support this claim about M3814 effects in T cells.

claim: When HDR donor was present, the rate of large deletions was not increased with NHEJ inhibition.
source: Importantly for safety, the 53BP1 study also showed that while NHEJ inhibition increased the rate of large deletions in the absence of HDR donor, when HDR donor was present the rate of large deletions was not increased, nor was the rate of off-target edits (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this safety claim about NHEJ inhibition.

claim: The rate of off-target edits was not increased with NHEJ inhibition when HDR donor was present.
source: Importantly for safety, the 53BP1 study also showed that while NHEJ inhibition increased the rate of large deletions in the absence of HDR donor, when HDR donor was present the rate of large deletions was not increased, nor was the rate of off-target edits (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this safety claim about off-target edits.

claim: A 48 hr pre-stimulation in growth factor mixture induces even the most primitive phenotypic HSC to cycle by ~66 hr.
source: As a basis for our protocol (Figure 1A), we used a 48 hr pre-stimulation in a growth factor mixture of SCF, FLT3L, IL3, and IL6 which we have previously shown induces even the most primitive phenotypic HSC to cycle by ~66 hr (Knapp et al., 2017), thus ensuring that editing machinery would be present during S/G2 phase of the cells.
evidence: The results section cites the authors' previous work (Knapp et al., 2017) to support this claim about cell cycle induction.

claim: UM171 improves the maintenance of HSC functional capacity.
source: We also included UM171, which improves the maintenance of HSC functional capacity (Fares et al., 2014) and can improve transduction efficiency in these cells (Ngom et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section cites published literature (Fares et al., 2014) to support this claim about UM171 effects.

claim: UM171 can improve transduction efficiency in HSPCs.
source: We also included UM171, which improves the maintenance of HSC functional capacity (Fares et al., 2014) and can improve transduction efficiency in these cells (Ngom et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section cites published literature (Ngom et al., 2018) to support this claim about UM171 effects on transduction.

claim: At lower RNP concentrations, there was a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer.
source: At lower RNP concentrations, we observed a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer, though this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR = 0.02 and FDR = 0.48, respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR values) to support this claim.

claim: Increasing RNP concentration showed a benefit to overall editing efficiency.
source: Similarly, increasing RNP concentration also showed a benefit to overall editing efficiency (FDR = 0.08, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) to support this claim.

claim: Both the addition of an electroporation enhancer and the increase in RNP concentration resulted in significantly decreased cell numbers indicating toxicity.
source: Both the addition of an electroporation enhancer and the increase in RNP concentration, however, resulted in significantly decreased cell numbers indicating toxicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data showing decreased cell numbers to support this toxicity claim.

claim: A nested PCR was required to avoid non-specific amplification from non-integrated AAV donors.
source: One critical factor we discovered here was that for this assessment a nested PCR was required with outer primers outside the homology arms of the AAV, as otherwise non-specific amplification from non-integrated donors predominated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A demonstrating the need for nested PCR.

claim: The BspEI-based assay is accurate down to ~1% integration efficiency.
source: Using defined mixtures of WT and BspEI DNA, we show that this assay is accurate down to ~1% integration efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B demonstrating assay accuracy.

claim: For AAV, a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 400 MOI gave the highest integration rate prior to observable toxicity with an integration rate of 19.8%.
source: For AAV, a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 400 MOI gave the highest integration rate prior to observable toxicity with an integration rate of 19.8% (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1C and D to support this claim about optimal AAV MOI.

claim: Short ssODN donors showed an integration rate of 12% at 50 pmol.
source: For these, 100 ng of amplified DNA was added to 1 x NEBuffer 3.1 with 2 U BspEI. These were then incubated at 37 °C for 1 hr and then run on a 2% TAE agarose gel with GelRed and quantified by densitometry. For AAV donors, these were run directly on a gel, and integration quantified based on the size shift from the introduced 143 bp synthetic intron. Finally, for ssODN with silent mutations, PCR products were purified by GeneJet PCR purification, quantified by nanodrop, and 5–15 ng sent for Sanger sequencing at the IRIC Genomics core with the primer pri0003-A1 (Key Resource Table). Integration was then quantified using ICE Analysis (Synthego Performance Analysis, 2019. v3.0. Synthego) with a comparison between each edited sample back to a matched unedited control.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E to support this claim about ssODN integration rate.

claim: Toxicity for both ssODN donors was independent of the presence of the Cas9 nuclease.
source: Interestingly, toxicity for both ssODN donors was independent of the presence of the Cas9 nuclease (equivalent in the no RNP condition), suggesting that it is likely an innate immune reaction to the single-stranded DNA rather than the editing process itself.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1F and provides an interpretation based on the observation.

claim: An increased HDR efficiency up to 70% was observed with M3814.
source: We observed an increased HDR efficiency up to 70% with M3814 (Figure 2A), equivalent to reports with inhibition of 53BP1 (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2A to support this claim about M3814 effects.

claim: AZD7648 has been reported to inhibit DNA-PK with reduced off-target activity on PI3K.
source: We also tested another DNA-PK inhibitor AZD7648 which has been reported to inhibit DNA-PK with reduced off-target activity on PI3K (Fok et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section cites published literature (Fok et al., 2019) to support this claim about AZD7648 specificity.

claim: Improved editing efficiency was observed at 0.5 µM with AZD7648 compared to M3814.
source: Interestingly, we observed improved editing efficiency at 0.5 µM with AZD7648 compared to M3814, and 0.5 µM AZD7648 was equivalent to 5 µM M3814 (Figure 2A, FDR = 0.01 and FDR = 0.24, respectively).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR values) in Figure 2A to support this claim.

claim: Toxicity was marginally but statistically significantly lower for AZD7648 compared to M3814 at 0.5 µM.
source: Toxicity, as assessed by viable cell counts, was also marginally but statistically significantly lower for AZD7648 compared to M3814 at 0.5 µM (Figure 2B, FDR = 0.02 for 0.5 µM).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) in Figure 2B to support this claim.

claim: The addition of RS1 either alone or together with AZD7648 was detrimental to editing efficiency and toxic to cells.
source: In this context, the addition of RS1 either alone or together with AZD7648 was detrimental to editing efficiency and toxic to cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2C to support this claim about RS1 effects.

claim: The combination of p53siRNA and AZD7648 was able to achieve mean efficiencies of 80% and up to 96%.
source: The combination of p53siRNA and AZD7648, however, was able to achieve mean efficiencies of 80% and up to 96% in these tests with minimal toxicity (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2C and D to support this claim about combined effects.

claim: The number of conditions tested in each experiment was related to editing efficiency.
source: A closer examination of experimental factors that may affect efficiency revealed this to be related to the number of conditions tested in each experiment (Figure 2E).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2E showing a correlation between condition number and efficiency.

claim: There are likely technical factors associated with cell handling and nucleofection timing that play an important role in overall efficiency.
source: This suggests that there are likely technical factors associated with cell handling and nucleofection timing that play an important role in overall efficiency.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the observed correlation between condition number and efficiency.

claim: A mean efficiency of 97% with AAV donors was observed in tests performed with no more than four simultaneous conditions at nucleofection.
source: Confirming our observed negative correlation between condition number and efficiency, in these tests performed with no more than four simultaneous conditions at nucleofection, we observed a mean efficiency of 97% with AAV donors (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about AAV efficiency.

claim: The incorporation of additional spacer-breaking mutations drastically improved editing efficiency up to 94% for ssODN donors.
source: Interestingly, the incorporation of these additional spacer-breaking mutations drastically improved editing efficiency up to 94%, nearly that of the AAV (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about spacer mutation effects.

claim: The design incorporating only the silent spacer mutations, but no PAM mutation achieved a mean efficiency of 84%.
source: Surprisingly, even the design incorporating only the silent spacer mutations, but no PAM mutation achieved a mean efficiency of 84%, further highlighting the importance of spacer mutations in donor design.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G to support this claim about silent mutation effects.

claim: No detectable edits were found at the top 3 predicted off-target sites either with or without AZD7648.
source: Analysis of the top 3 predicted off-target sites in 3 sets of samples revealed no detectable edits at these sites either with or without AZD7648 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2H and supplements to support this claim about off-target editing.

claim: Off-target editing at predicted sites is not affected by AZD7648 addition, at least with well-designed gRNA.
source: This suggests that off-target editing at predicted sites is not affected by AZD7648 addition, at least with well-designed gRNA.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the off-target analysis data.

claim: No significant differences in editing efficiencies from bulk measurements were observed regardless of sub-population.
source: We observed no significant differences in editing efficiencies from bulk measurements regardless of sub-population suggesting that the editing was even across the progenitor hierarchy (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3A to support this claim about editing across the hierarchy.

claim: A slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of CD34+ cells of the advanced progenitor phenotype.
source: We also observed a generally equivalent representation of each population within the CD34 compartment between silent edited and control cells, though a slight but statistically significant decrease was observed in the proportion of CD34 + cells of the advanced progenitor phenotype (FDR = 0.007; Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis (FDR value) in Figure 3B to support this claim.

claim: A slight drop in colony number was observed even without editing, consistent with donor-induced toxicity.
source: Consistent with our earlier observations that donor alone induced some toxicity, we observed a slight drop in colony number even without editing (Figure 3D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3D and relates it to earlier observations.

claim: Colony number was further decreased with editing.
source: Colony number was further decreased with editing (Figure 3D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3D to support this claim about editing effects on colony number.

claim: No changes to colony type were observed with editing.
source: Importantly, however, no changes to colony type were observed (Figure 3E), suggesting that while there is a quantitative drop in progenitor function, this was even across progenitor types and the capability of remaining cells was not affected.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3E to support this claim about colony type distribution.

claim: Colonies showed a preponderance of homozygous edits.
source: Analysis of the editing on colonies revealed editing across most colonies with a predominance of homozygous edits (Figure 3F), as expected by our high editing efficiencies.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3F to support this claim about zygosity in colonies.

claim: There was no significant difference in the frequency of highly proliferative clones between edited cells and non-edited controls.
source: Critically, there was no significant difference in the frequency of highly proliferative clones between edited cells and non-edited controls (Figure 3I), suggesting that the editing process does not substantially affect the most regenerative subset of HSC.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3I with statistical analysis to support this claim about LTC-IC frequency.

claim: There was a trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation and transient clones in the edited condition.
source: While there was not a significant difference, there was a trend towards lower frequencies of low proliferation and transient clones in the edited condition (Figure 3I).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 3I showing a non-significant trend.

claim: A highly significant monotonic decrease in mutant allele frequency was observed with increasing silent donor proportion.
source: At 48 hr post editing a bulk sample was harvested to determine overall editing efficiency. This showed a highly significant monotonic decrease in mutant allele frequency with increasing silent donor proportion (p<<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis in Figure 4B to support this claim about tunable zygosity.

claim: No significant differences in clonogenic efficiency were observed across conditions in the zygosity tuning experiments.
source: No significant differences in clonogenic efficiency were observed across conditions though there were no large clones (i.e. in excess of 100 cells) in the 100% mutant donor condition (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 4C to support this claim about clonogenic efficiency.

claim: A preponderance of homozygous edits was observed with all mutant donors, with a progressive increase in heterozygous or homozygous silent as the proportion of silent donor was increased.
source: As expected, we observed a preponderance of homozygous edits with all mutant donors, with a progressive increase in heterozygous or homozygous silent as the proportion of silent donor was increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 4D to support this claim about zygosity distribution.

claim: AZD7648 is optimal for improving HDR efficiency in HSPCs, consistent with demonstrations of its improved potency and specificity.
source: Through these tests, we confirmed reports that DNA-PK inhibition was an effective method to improve HDR efficiency (De Ravin et al., 2021; Shy et al., 2023), and identified AZD7648 to be optimal for this task, consistent with demonstrations of its improved potency and specificity (Fok et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Fok et al., 2019) and relates it to the experimental findings.

claim: Additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence were necessary to achieve maximal efficiencies with ssODN donors.
source: The difference is likely attributable to the design of the ssODN donors themselves, as we also found that additional silent mutations in the spacer sequence were necessary to achieve maximal efficiencies.
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation based on the experimental findings comparing ssODN designs.

claim: Most AAV donors insert a tag of some description, providing a spacer disruption built-in to these systems.
source: Given that most AAV donors insert a tag of some description (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2022; De Ravin et al., 2021), such a spacer disruption has been built-in to these systems, but not in the competing ssODN.
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2022; De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about AAV donor design.

claim: The number of conditions simultaneously processed at the time of nucleofection had a substantial effect on efficiency.
source: One surprising factor that had a substantial effect on efficiency was the number of conditions simultaneously processed at the time of nucleofection.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental finding about condition number effects.

claim: The effect of condition number on efficiency likely corresponds to the handling time.
source: This likely corresponds to the handling time, and may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection previously reported (Charlesworth et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation and cites published literature (Charlesworth et al., 2018) to support this inference.

claim: Editing did not change the frequency of populations across the hematopoietic hierarchy.
source: To ensure that the editing process was functional throughout the hierarchy, and not specifically toxic to specific levels, we demonstrated that editing did not change the frequency of populations across this hierarchy and that editing efficiency was equivalent throughout, including in the HSC phenotype.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about editing across the hierarchy.

claim: Editing did not alter the distribution of myeloid outputs in clonogenic assays.
source: Beyond this, using clonogenic assays for progenitor differentiation, we demonstrated that editing did not alter the distribution of myeloid outputs.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about myeloid differentiation.

claim: Previous reports demonstrated that editing rates were consistent in pre-transplant measured and post-transplantation both with and without DNA-PK inhibition.
source: These findings together with previous reports demonstrating that editing rates were consistent in pre-transplant measured and post-transplantation both with and without DNA-PK inhibition (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) suggest that the reported editing protocol also edited cells capable of engrafting a mouse for >6 months (functional long-term HSC).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Bak et al., 2018; Charlesworth et al., 2018; Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about editing consistency.

claim: A modest decrease in CFC potential was observed with editing.
source: We did, however, observe a modest decrease in CFC potential and a non-significant trend towards the same in low proliferation LTC-IC, suggesting that late progenitors may be more sensitive to the editing process than the most primitive.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about CFC and LTC-IC effects.

claim: Much of the toxicity both in direct cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery, regardless of editing.
source: It is important to note, however, that our and others' data suggest that remaining CFCs appear to retain normal function (Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021). Interestingly, much of the toxicity both in direct cell survival and CFC numbers could be attributed to donor delivery, regardless of editing.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings and cites published literature (Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021) about toxicity sources.

claim: Toxicity is likely mediated by innate immune responses to DNA.
source: This suggests that toxicity is likely mediated by innate immune responses to DNA (Piras and Kajaste-Rudnitski, 2021).
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation and cites published literature (Piras and Kajaste-Rudnitski, 2021) to support this inference.

claim: No off-target edits were observed at predicted sites, regardless of whether edits were done in the presence of AZD7648/p53 siRNA or not.
source: We did not observe any off-target edits at predicted sites, regardless of whether edits were done in the presence of AZD7648/p53 siRNA or not, suggesting that the protocol presented here did not substantially increase off-target editing frequencies.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the experimental findings about off-target editing.

claim: No increases in off target editing or large-scale genomic rearrangements were observed when donor was present with 53BP1 inhibition.
source: This was consistent with findings from other studies using 53BP1 inhibition which similarly targets NHEJ, where they observed no increases in off target editing or large-scale genomic rearrangements were observed when donor was present (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim about safety with NHEJ inhibition.

claim: Another manuscript showed similar effects for the addition of AZD7648 as being able to increase the precise editing efficiency of human HSPCs.
source: During the time that this article was undergoing its publication process, another manuscript came out showing similar effects for the addition of AZD7648 as being able to increase the precise editing efficiency of human HSPCs (as well as T and B cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells) (Selvaraj et al., 2024).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to support this claim about AZD7648 effects in other studies.

claim: The other manuscript showed an increase in efficiency to similar levels using AAV6 donors.
source: In their manuscript they also show an increase in efficiency to similar levels using AAV6 donors, and similar but slightly lower inefficiencies that we achieved in ssODN donors (Selvaraj et al., 2024).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings.

claim: The differences in ssODN efficiency are likely attributable to the use of shorter ssODN donors and choice of silent spacer disrupting mutations.
source: The differences are likely attributable to our use of shorter ssODN donors and our choice of silent spacer disrupting mutations in them.
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation comparing the current study to another published work.

claim: Both ssODN donor length and silent spacer disrupting mutations have been previously shown to impact the integration efficiency.
source: Both of these factors have been previously shown to impact the integration efficiency (Okamoto et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Okamoto et al., 2019) to support this claim about factors affecting integration.

claim: Similar viability effects of AAV donor and lack of negative effects from 0.5 µM AZD7648 were observed in another study.
source: We also observed similar viability effects of AAV donor, and lack of negative effects from 0.5 µM AZD7648 (Selvaraj et al., 2024), though we extend this with the effects of the ssODN donors and ssODN donor length on viability.
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings about viability.

claim: Another study similarly showed that CFC distributions are not affected by the editing process.
source: Again, we similarly show that CFC distributions are not affected by the editing process (Selvaraj et al., 2024), though we again extend this with information on the effect of ssODN donors on total CFC frequency.
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Selvaraj et al., 2024) to compare findings about CFC distributions.

claim: Another article used AZD7648 together with Polθ inhibitors in several non-hematopoietic cell lines to improve editing efficiency.
source: Finally, another article was also published while we were in our review process in which they used AZD7648 together with Polθ inhibitors in several non-hematopoietic cell lines to improve editing efficiency (Wimberger et al., 2023).
evidence: The discussion cites published literature (Wimberger et al., 2023) to reference related work.

claim: The P95H mutation in SRSF2 is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and clonal hematopoiesis.
source: Of note, the PAM mutation in our mutant donors introduces a P95H mutation which is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and clonal hematopoiesis (Watson et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2011; van der Werf et al., 2021).
evidence: The results section cites published literature (Watson et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2011; van der Werf et al., 2021) to support this claim about the P95H mutation.

claim: Clones with high proliferative potential at 8 weeks in the LTC-IC assay correlate with those HSC with the highest regenerative potential in vivo.
source: We have previously shown that clones with high proliferative potential at 8 weeks in this assay correlate with those HSC with the highest regenerative potential in vivo (Knapp et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section cites the authors' previous work (Knapp et al., 2018) to support this claim about LTC-IC assay predictive value.

claim: Phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells.
source: While phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019), not all of these markers are stable on cultured cells.
evidence: The results section cites published literature (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019) to support this claim about CD49f marker selectivity.

claim: Cell density was maintained below 250,000 cells/mL of total media to prevent auto-inhibition of the primitive cells.
source: Cell density was maintained below 250,000 cells/mL of total media to prevent auto-inhibition of the primitive cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Csaszar et al., 2012).
evidence: The methods section cites published literature (Knapp et al., 2017; Csaszar et al., 2012) to support this culture condition.

claim: At lower RNP concentrations, the electroporation enhancer benefit was not present at higher concentrations.
source: At lower RNP concentrations, we observed a slight benefit of the addition of an electroporation enhancer, though this was not present at higher concentrations (FDR = 0.02 and FDR = 0.48, respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis to support this claim about concentration-dependent effects.

claim: 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer was selected for subsequent experiments.
source: As the improvements in cutting efficiency, while statistically significant, were only in the range of ~10% and both increased toxicity, we selected 30.5 pmol RNP without enhancer for subsequent experiments.
evidence: The results section describes the decision-making process based on experimental data.

claim: Long ssODN donors showed a very low integration efficiency of 3% at 20 pmol and a high toxicity.
source: While the long ssODN donors showed a very low integration efficiency of 3% at 20 pmol and a high toxicity, short ssODN donors were more promising with an integration rate of 12% at 50 pmol and a lesser though still appreciable toxicity (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E and F to support this claim about long ssODN performance.

claim: Higher concentrations of short ssODN further raised efficiency though with a corresponding increase in toxicity beyond a usable range.
source: Higher concentrations of short ssODN further raised efficiency though with a corresponding increase in toxicity beyond a usable range (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 1E and F to support this claim about dose-response effects.

claim: The AAV donor at 400 MOI and short ssODN at 50 pmol are the most suitable donors.
source: These data demonstrate that the AAV donor at 400 MOI and short ssODN at 50 pmol are the most suitable donors.
evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing different donor types and concentrations.

claim: There was no significant difference in editing efficiency for AZD7648 at 0.5 and 5 µM.
source: There was also no significant difference in editing efficiency for AZD7648 at 0.5 and 5 µM but a slight improvement in viability (FDR = 0.16 and FDR = 0.01, respectively Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis in Figure 2A and B to support this claim about AZD7648 dose effects.

claim: Repeating tests on the SF3B1 locus revealed similar trends, though with a somewhat lower mean editing efficiency of 57%.
source: Repeating these tests on the SF3B1 locus revealed similar trends, though with a somewhat lower mean editing efficiency of 57% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B to support this claim about locus-specific effects.

claim: The lower efficiency at SF3B1 reflects the lower cutting efficiency observed at this locus.
source: This difference reflects the lower cutting efficiency observed at this locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The results section relates the editing efficiency to cutting efficiency data from earlier experiments.

claim: Limiting the number of co-processed samples can substantially improve editing to near perfect efficiencies.
source: Overall, these data suggest that limiting the number of co-processed samples, and the addition of 0.5 µM AZD7648 for the 48 hr following editing could substantially improve editing to near perfect efficiencies.
evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the experimental data about factors affecting efficiency.

claim: With the short ssODN, a mean editing efficiency of 44% was observed under optimal conditions.
source: With the short ssODN, we observed a mean editing efficiency of 44% under these conditions, increased from the 13% but still substantially lower than AAV (Figure 2F and G), and consistent with reports for 53BP1 inhibition (De Ravin et al., 2021).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data in Figure 2G and cites published literature (De Ravin et al., 2021) to support this claim.

claim: The difference between AAV and ssODN efficiency was likely due to the further disruption of the spacer sequence provided by the synthetic intron in the AAV donor.
source: Further thought into the differences between the two suggested that perhaps it was the further disruption of the spacer sequence provided by the synthetic intron in the AAV donor which provided the difference (Figure 2F).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on comparison of donor designs.

claim: Some substitutions were present both in and around the predicted off-target regions, however, these were equivalent for a given individual between both edited conditions (+/-AZD7568) and unmanipulated controls.
source: Some substitutions were present both in and around the predicted off-target regions, however, these were equivalent for a given individual between both edited conditions (+/-AZD7568) and unmanipulated controls (paired t-test FDRs >0.3, individual values in Supplementary file 1) indicating they were not introduced by the editing process.
evidence: The results section presents experimental data with statistical analysis to support this claim about background substitutions.

claim: Phenotypes involving CD49f are not all stable on cultured cells.
source: While phenotypes involving CD49f are highly selective on fresh cells (Knapp et al., 2017; Notta et al., 2011; Knapp et al., 2019), not all of these markers are stable on cultured cells.
evidence: The results section cites published literature and provides additional context about marker stability.

claim: The panel used for sorting consisted of only culture-stable markers which retained the ability to sort sub-populations from across the hierarchy.
source: As such, we used a panel consisting of only culture-stable markers which retained the ability to sort sub-populations from across the hierarchy.

claim: The decrease in advanced progenitor phenotype is consistent with the slight drop in colony number.
source: This is consistent with the observed decrease in CFC frequency (Figure 3D), suggesting that later progenitors may be more affected by editing than the most primitive subsets.
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation connecting two experimental observations.

claim: Overall editing efficiencies in the zygosity tuning tests were lower than normal due to the requirement of simultaneously editing many conditions.
source: It should be noted that overall editing efficiencies in these tests were lower than normal due to the requirement of simultaneously editing many conditions.
evidence: The results section provides context for the experimental results based on earlier observations about condition number effects.

claim: The analysis of zygosity was not confounded by differential clonogenicity of specific mutational statuses.
source: These results suggest that this analysis was not confounded by differential clonogenicity of specific mutational statuses (homozygous WT/silent, heterozygous, homozygous mutant).
evidence: The results section provides an interpretation based on the clonogenic efficiency data.

claim: Desired zygosity ratios could be predicted based on simple sampling calculations.
source: Desired zygosity ratios could thus be predicted based on simple sampling calculations.
evidence: The results section provides a conclusion based on the observed linear relationship between donor ratio and zygosity.

claim: The current study demonstrates a near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPC.
source: The current study demonstrates a near-perfect efficiency of precise editing in primary human HSPC and identifies the key design and technical considerations needed to achieve it.

claim: The current study identifies the key design and technical considerations needed to achieve near-perfect editing efficiency.

source: This simple design change facilitates the use of these much cheaper, faster to iterate, and more stable donors.

claim: The handling time effect may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection.
source: This likely corresponds to the handling time, and may be analogous to the delivery window for AAV immediately post-nucleofection previously reported (Charlesworth et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation and cites published literature to support the inference.

source: We did, however, observe a modest decrease in CFC potential and a non-significant trend towards the same in low proliferation LTC-IC, suggesting that late progenitors may be more sensitive to the editing process than the most primitive.
evidence: The discussion provides an interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: Remaining CFCs appear to retain normal function after editing.
source: It is important to note, however, that our and others' data suggest that remaining CFCs appear to retain normal function (Lehnertz et al., 2021; De Ravin et al., 2021).

claim: Interference with innate immune pathways may be a fruitful avenue to mitigate toxicity.

source: We did not observe any off-target edits at predicted sites, regardless of whether edits were done in the presence of AZD7648/p53 siRNA or not, suggesting that the protocol presented here did not substantially increase off-target editing frequencies.
evidence: The discussion provides a conclusion based on the off-target analysis data.

claim: The editing process and addition of AZD7648 edits evenly across the HSPC hierarchy.
source: Beyond what was done in the other manuscript, we also show that the editing process and addition of AZD7648 edits evenly across the HSPC hierarchy, and that it does not substantially affect the distribution of progenitor phenotypes and critically does not affect the LTC-ICs with the highest self-renewal potential.
